explanations.explanation: Judge is the word, friend. Paul, who wrote this letter, says let no one judge you by what you eat or drink. He even adds a feast, a New Moon or a Sabbath to the list. So when somebody squints at your plate, you may keep right on chewing.

Praise sounds so much nicer, friend, but it's not the word in this verse. Paul, who wrote this letter, says let no one judge you by what you eat or drink. Nobody is handing out gold stars for your lunch here. It's about people sizing you up over food and drink, and he says don't let them.

Reward would be a sweet deal, a cookie for every meal, but that's not what the verse says. Paul, who wrote this letter, says let no one judge you by what you eat or drink. The word is judge. Nobody gets to hold a scorecard over your plate.

True! Paul, who wrote this letter, puts a Sabbath on the list right beside a feast and a New Moon. His words are, “Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath.” That's a whole list, friend, and not one seat on it for a scorekeeper.

This one is true, friend, and the Sabbath is right there in the verse. Paul, who wrote this letter, says, “Therefore let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath.” It sits in a list with a feast and a New Moon. Easy to blink and miss when the list is that long.

Christ! Paul says these things are a shadow of the things to come, and then says “…the body that casts it belongs to Christ.” A shadow tells you something real is standing nearby. Friend, you don't hug the shadow when the real One is right there.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, so I get why it jumped out. But Paul says “…the body that casts it belongs to Christ.” The shadow is food, drink, feasts, New Moons and Sabbaths, and the body behind it is Christ's. Keep your eyes on the One casting it, friend.

Aaron was the brother of Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 4:14), and he's a good guess. But that's not who Paul names here. He says the shadow is cast by a body, and “…the body that casts it belongs to Christ.” Good name, wrong shadow, friend.

Disqualify, friend! Paul says not to let the person who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you with speculation about what he has seen. Speculation is just guessing. A guess shouldn't get to bench anybody.

Comfort would be lovely, but this fella isn't tucking anybody in. Paul says not to let him disqualify you with speculation about what he has seen. I think a warm blanket would have been a lot nicer, friend. The verse is about being disqualified.

Forgiving is a beautiful thing, and I'm a big fan. But that's not what this verse is about. Paul warns that this person might disqualify you with speculation about what he has seen. So the word to catch is disqualify, friend.

Close, friend, but the verse turns it around. It says, “Such a person is puffed up without basis by his unspiritual mind.” Unspiritual, not very spiritual. Puffed up, and with nothing under it. That's a lot of air for nothing.
False! The verse says, “Such a person is puffed up without basis by his unspiritual mind.” He's puffed up, and Paul says there's no basis for it. Friend, that's a lot of puff with nothing underneath.

The head, friend! Paul says, “He has lost connection to the head…” and the head is where the whole body gets its support. Elsewhere Paul writes that Christ is the head of the body, the church (Colossians 1:18). Cut off from the head, nothing else is going to work.

Feet do a lot of hard work, friend, but they aren't the ones in this verse. Paul says, “He has lost connection to the head…” The whole body gets supported and knit together from the head. Nobody tells the head to take a seat and let the feet handle it.

Hands are handy, I'll give them that. But Paul says, “He has lost connection to the head…” The head is where the whole body is supported and knit together by its joints and ligaments. Hands are great, friend, but they can't run this show.

God! Paul says the whole body is supported and knit together, and it “…grows as God causes it to grow.” The joints and ligaments do their part, but the growing is God's doing. Friend, that takes the pressure right off.
Paul wrote the letter, so I see why he came to mind. But he doesn't take the job for himself. He says the body “…grows as God causes it to grow.” Humble man, friend.

Angels do show up in this passage, but only as something the false humility person worships. When it comes to the growing, Paul says the body “…grows as God causes it to grow.” So the growing isn't handed to angels, friend. It's God's doing.

Regulations, friend! Paul asks, “…why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its regulations” after dying with Christ to the spiritual forces of the world. That's a pointed question. And the very next verse shows the kind of rules he means.

Armies sounds dramatic, I know. But the rules Paul has in mind are things like “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!” The question is why they'd still submit to the world's regulations. Friend, that's a rulebook, not a battlefield.

Kings would have been a bold twist, friend, but that's not the word. Paul asks why they'd still submit to the world's regulations, and the next verse gives the sample: “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!” Those are rules, not rulers.
Perish! Paul says, “These will all perish with use…” Rules like that don't hold up the way they seem to. Use them and they wear out, friend, like a paper plate at a family reunion.
Multiply is what dough does on my apron, friend, but not what Paul says here. He says, “These will all perish with use…” Those rules don't grow. They wear out.
Rules that get better the more you use them would be nice, friend. But Paul says, “These will all perish with use…” Using them doesn't polish them up. It wears them out.

Human commands and teachings, friend! Paul says these rules will perish with use, “…they are based on human commands and teachings.” That's where they come from. People made them up, and that's a shaky place to build from.

I understand why you might lean this way, friend, but Paul says no. He says these rules perish with use, “…they are based on human commands and teachings.” They come from people, not from Christ. Good thing he spelled it out.

The prophets are a solid name, friend, but Paul doesn't bring them up here. He says these rules perish with use, “…they are based on human commands and teachings.” So he traces them back to people. Same as a recipe somebody scribbled on a napkin and swore was official.

Close, friend, but Paul says the opposite. He says these restrictions have an appearance of wisdom, “…but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.” They look good and carry no real value there. Pretty wrapper, empty box.

False! Paul says these restrictions have an appearance of wisdom, “…but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh.” Self-prescribed worship, false humility and harsh treatment of the body might look impressive. Friend, looking wise and being wise are two different things.
